summary: Registers and documents the haptics top-level media type, under which subtypes for representing haptic data can be registered. It also registers several subtypes that reflect existing practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Media types label the kind of content carried over the Internet, such as 'audio' or 'video'. This RFC adds 'haptics' as a top-level media type for data that describes touch sensations, and registers three formats under it: ivs, hjif and hmpg.

subtitle: Touch gets a top-level media type of its own, with three haptic formats registered under it.

tldr.problem: Haptic data, the instructions that make a device vibrate or push back, had no registered home among Internet media types, and no existing top-level type fitted it well.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers 'haptics' as a top-level media type following the rules in RFC 9694, says unknown subtypes should be treated as 'application/octet-stream', and registers three subtypes: 'ivs', 'hjif' and 'hmpg'.
tldr.outcome: Haptic formats can now be registered as 'haptics' followed by a subtype name. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9993.

today: RFC 9695 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025, and it has since been updated by RFC 9993. It registers the top-level type and three subtypes; further haptic formats can be added later as new subtypes under 'haptics'.

sections.title: What Haptics Is and Why It Needs a Type
sections.content:
Haptics means generating touch-related sensations in a device or interface. The most common use is in mobile devices, where haptics gives feedback to a person using the touchscreen, for example when typing on a virtual keyboard.

Haptic technologies differ from audio and visual ones because they need some form of actuation to create a tactile sensation. In mobile phones and game controllers the actuator is typically a small vibrating motor. In large touchscreens in vehicles the actuator can be a specialized piezoelectric material. Haptic capabilities are found in nearly every modern smartphone, game and virtual reality controller.

Internet media types, as defined in RFC 6838, label content carried over Internet protocols. This RFC defines a new top-level type, haptics, following the guidelines in RFC 9694. The type signals that the content specifies haptic data, and different representation formats of haptics can be registered beneath it.
sections.plainLanguage: Haptics is the feel of touch, produced by something that moves or vibrates. A media type is the label that says what kind of data a file holds. This RFC adds 'haptics' as that label for data that describes touch sensations.

sections.title: Formats and Devices That Already Exist
sections.content:
Haptic signals add a layer of sensation to audio and video. Haptic tracks held in separate files can be played back in sync with audio and video files to give an immersive media experience. More recently, haptic tracks embedded in the ISO Base Media File Format (ISOBMFF) enable the haptic signals to be played over one or more actuators at the same time as the audio and video. Haptic signals are also part of media streams that use RTP, such as streams for games, XR and wearables.

Haptics was proposed as a first-order media type, at the same level as audio and video, inside ISOBMFF in April 2020. The proposal has since progressed to International Standard and was published in January 2022, which places haptics in the ISO/IEC 14496-12 (ISOBMFF) standard, 7th Edition. The RFC argues that this is a strong case for adding haptics to the top-level media types recognized by the IETF, and it sketches how mp4 files would be labelled once the type is registered: haptics/mp4 for mp4 files with only haptic tracks, video/mp4 for mp4 files with video, audio and haptics, and audio/mp4 for mp4 files with audio and haptics.

The RFC also argues from uptake. It cites 231+ million iPhone units sold in 2023 with built-in support for haptic-encoded data, 1.27+ billion Android units sold in 2023 with API support for haptic buffers, 45+ million game console units sold in 2023, and 30+ million XR device units sold in 2023 with an OpenXR haptic API. The W3C has a vibration API that mobile browsers may support, and vibration extensions for gamepads.
sections.plainLanguage: Haptic files already exist in devices that people buy every day, and the file format for audio and video now has a defined place for touch data. The RFC uses that existing use to argue that haptics deserves its own media type.

sections.title: The Sub-Modalities of Haptics
sections.content:
The RFC lists several sub-modalities of haptics: vibrotactile, which is touch or vibration; kinesthetic, which is force feedback; surface, which is surface friction; spatial, non-contact, which is ultrasound; and thermal, which is temperature.

Because these sub-modalities sit under one top-level type, formats for each of them can be defined in a streamlined way. The RFC states that this would not be possible if 'haptics' were placed under another top-level type such as 'audio', 'video' or 'application'.

The RFC also argues from the human senses: 'audio' stands for the sense of hearing and 'video' for the sense of seeing, so it makes sense for the sense of touch to be represented by its own top-level type. Placing 'haptics' under 'audio' or 'video' would not reflect the kinds of files and use cases that need haptics but have nothing to do with audio or video.
sections.plainLanguage: Touch comes in several forms: vibration, force, friction, ultrasound and heat. Giving haptics its own top-level type lets formats for each form be named in one place.

sections.title: Why Not Under the 'application' Type
sections.content: The RFC gives three reasons why 'haptics' does not fit under the 'application' top-level type. First, haptics connects to a sensory system, touch and motion, directly, and is more specific than the abstract 'application' type. Second, 'application' has historically been used for applications, that is, code, which means it is viewed and treated with great care for security, and 'haptics' is not code, just as 'audio' and 'video' are not code either. Third, haptics is a property of a media stream and not an application under any normal definition, so it should be its own type.
sections.plainLanguage: The 'application' type is reserved for programs, which get careful security treatment. Haptic data is media, not a program, and it belongs with the senses rather than with software.

sections.title: What the Type Means and How It Is Registered
sections.content:
The RFC defines 'haptics' as the primary media content type that indicates the content requires a haptics subsystem, such as low-level haptics APIs, which in turn requires hardware capabilities such as one or more actuators to render the haptics media. The type gives no specific information about the underlying data format or how the haptic information should be interpreted. The subtypes defined within a 'haptics' tree name the specific haptic formats.

Unrecognized subtypes of 'haptics' should be treated as application/octet-stream. An implementation may still pass an unrecognized subtype to the haptics subsystem and its rendering hardware.

For registration, new haptics formats should be requested using the IANA Application for a Media Type form, and RFC 6838 should be consulted on registration procedures. In particular, the haptics specification should preferably be freely available. New subtypes may define parameters, and an implementation that does not recognize a parameter sub-value in the comma-separated list should ignore that sub-value and continue processing the others.

IANA has registered 'haptics' in the 'Top-Level Media Types' registry defined in RFC 9694 and has registered several subtypes. IANA has also added 'haptics' as an alternative value of 'Type Name' in the media types registration form.
sections.plainLanguage: The 'haptics' label says the content needs a haptic subsystem and hardware that can produce touch. The subtype name says which file format it is. A file with an unknown haptic subtype should be treated as an opaque stream of bytes, though it may still be passed to the haptic hardware.

sections.title: The Three Registered Subtypes
sections.content:
The RFC registers three subtypes as the initial entries under the top-level 'haptics' type, and they serve as examples for later registrations. All three have no required and no optional parameters, and all three list the same applications: applications able to create, edit or display haptic media content. All three name ISO/IEC JTC1/SC 29/WG 7 (MPEG 3D Graphics and Haptic Coding) as change controller.

The ivs subtype is a device-independent haptic effect coding based on the XML format, designed to enable interoperability between distinct physical endpoints. Its encoding considerations are 8bit if UTF-8, and binary if UTF-16 or UTF-32. Its published specification is the ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/WG 2 document 'Encoder Input Format for MPEG Haptics', and its file extension is .ivs. The RFC notes that not all devices may be able to render all effects present in an IVS file.

The hjif subtype is a human-readable haptic effect coding based on the JSON format, designed as an interchange format for temporal and spatial haptic effects. The effects may target specific parts of the human body and may be associated with a reference device description, which lets haptic rendering software adapt the effects to the hardware available. Its published specification is ISO/IEC 23090-31, Haptics coding, its encoding considerations are 8bit if UTF-8 and binary if UTF-16 or UTF-32, and its file extension is .hjif.

The hmpg subtype is a streamable binary haptic effect coding, designed for efficient coding of temporal and spatial haptic effects. Like hjif, its effects may target specific parts of the human body and may carry a reference device description. Its published specification is ISO/IEC 23090-31, Haptics coding, its encoding considerations are binary, and its file extension is .hmpg.
sections.plainLanguage: Three formats are registered under 'haptics'. IVS is an XML format for device-independent effects, HJIF is a JSON format meant for exchanging effects between systems, and HMPG is a compact binary format for streaming them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Haptics are interpreted data structures that represent collections of media rendering instructions, intended to be decoded and rendered on target device hardware. Haptic data can be collections of signal data, descriptive text in XML or JSON, or both. Signal data is typically not executed by endpoint processors and represents minimal security risk. Descriptive text is typically parsed and represented in memory using standard XML data structures, and is then used to construct one or more signals sent to the device hardware.

Because of the media and rendering nature of the data path, the security profile of haptic data is expected to be largely consistent with that of visual and audio media data. As with any synthesized media data, there is a risk in executing commands based on a descriptive encoding, either through its inherent extensibility or through arbitrary executable data inserted into the descriptive format. Media rendering systems are normally implemented with a mix of user and kernel space execution, because the media must reach a hardware system, so malicious instructions in descriptive haptic media have the potential to execute arbitrary code in kernel space and bypass system permission structures or execution sandboxes.

The RFC notes that haptics, audio and video media have widespread use, and that operating system and device driver implementors should pay careful attention to ensure that synthesis and rendering signal paths do not provide attack surfaces for malicious payloads. Thermal devices, which give a sensation of heat, and kinesthetic devices, which give force feedback, could potentially injure users if the heat or force is not properly controlled or inadvertently exceeds safety levels, so implementors need adequate measures to prevent that. These considerations apply to the subtype registrations in this document and to all future haptics registrations.
sections.plainLanguage: Haptic data is decoded by the device, so a malformed or hostile file could try to reach the operating system kernel. Devices that produce heat or force also have to keep those within safe limits so that they cannot hurt the person using them.
